newsitem.title: UK: British parliament launches new sleaze inquiry.
newsitem.headline: British parliament launches new sleaze inquiry.

text.p: Britain's Parliament ordered an inquiry on Wednesday into allegations that a member of the government tried to influence a probe into sleaze in the ruling Conservative Party.

A powerful parliamentary committee is to investigate whether David Willetts, now a junior minister, tried to influence an earlier probe into charges that a former minister broke rules of conduct by taking money for asking parliamentary questions.

The new inquiry was demanded by opposition parties after newspaper reports that Willetts, then a parliamentary business manager or "whip" for the ruling party, tried to get the inquiry into the so-called "cash-for-questions" scandal shelved.

Members of parliament overwhelmingly backed the call for a thorough inquiry by the Standards and Privileges Committee, which oversees the conduct of members, after Labour's Andrew Miller said parliament's reputation was at risk.
"If the alleged interference actually occurred we cannot hope to restore any of that public confidence in the integrity of this place unless we take firm, decisive action," he said.
The inquiry will be a severe political headache for Prime Minister John Major, lagging Labour by some 20 points in polls and with a general election now no more than seven months away.
But the government, fearing a public backlash, backed Labour's call for a thorough investigation.
The Conservatives have been in power for an unbroken 17 years and polls show voters are increasingly disillusioned with a government they see as riddled with sleaze and out of touch.

The message was driven home when rebel Conservative MP Peter Thurnham joined the minority Liberal Democrats at the weekend in protest at Major's handling of sleaze. Major now has a majority of just two in the House of Commons, parliament's lower chamber.

The latest inquiry goes back to allegations two years ago that former corporate affairs minister Neil Hamilton broke House of Commons rules by taking cash to ask questions and for failing to declare favours from Harrods boss Mohammed al Fayed, including a stay at the Paris Ritz hotel.
Another junior minister, Tim Smith, resigned after admitting he had taken cash to put parliamentary questions for Fayed.

Hamilton also quit, vowing to clear his name. But two weeks ago he dropped a libel action against the Guardian newspaper which broke the story, saying he could not afford the legal fees. The Guardian responded by printing fresh allegations.

It also reported a handwritten memo by Willetts suggesting that the parliamentary committee investigating Hamilton could shelve its inquiry or ensure it was dealt with as quickly as possible by "exploiting the good Tory (Conservative) majority".

The two main opposition parties -- Labour and the Liberal Democrats -- joined forces on Monday to demand a full inquiry. The Standards and Privileges Committee has already decided on an emergency investigation into the allegations against Hamilton.
